summary_html: A **state agency fails** to meet federal child-welfare performance standards, triggering **funding penalties** or corrective action under the CFSR or Single Audit Act.
authority_html:
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — performance oversight and penalties  
- **Single Audit Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 7501–7507)** — audit of federally funded programs  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — oversight authority for HHS/OIG

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding DHS made reasonable reunification efforts despite the absence of visitation the children refused, that clear and convincing evidence supported the jury's verdict, and that trial counsel was effective.
key_cases.relevance: The court applies the seventeen-month reunification-services ceiling and the fifteen-of-twenty-two-month filing duty that implement federal ASFA and Title IV-E requirements.
key_cases.quote: We find the district court did not abuse its discretion when it found that DHS made reasonable efforts toward reunification.

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
key_cases.holding: The court held that placing Indian children with their mothers after emergency removal from the father was a foster care placement triggering ICWA § 1912(d), and affirmed the finding that the State made active efforts by clear and convincing evidence before adjudication.
key_cases.relevance: Failing to apply § 1912(d) to a parent placement is the kind of ICWA compliance gap this decision corrects.
key_cases.quote: We find no reason why the same case-by-case review should not be applied when deciding if State has made the required active efforts in this foster care placement.

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a new trial, holding ICWA's active-efforts requirement did not apply because no existing Indian family relationship would be broken up, and alternatively that clear and convincing evidence showed active efforts were made and had failed.
key_cases.relevance: It applies Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl in Oklahoma and defines when an active-efforts omission is not a compliance failure at all.
key_cases.quote: we conclude § 1912(d) of ICWA is inapplicable because there was no relationship or Indian family entity to breakup

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that "domicile" in the Indian Child Welfare Act has a uniform federal meaning, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents are domiciled on the reservation, and that exclusive tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) therefore applied notwithstanding the parents' voluntary off-reservation surrender.
key_cases.relevance: A state court that proceeds where exclusive tribal jurisdiction exists has entered a void order, the most serious form of ICWA non-compliance.
key_cases.quote: Tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) was not meant to be defeated by the actions of individual members of the tribe

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of Baby Boy L.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed an order declaring an Indian child eligible for adoption without the father's consent, abandoning the judicially created existing Indian family exception in light of amendments to the Oklahoma ICWA and expressly overruling In re S.C., Baby Boy D and D.M.J.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Oklahoma authority that a state court may not decline to apply ICWA on the theory that no Indian family existed, the compliance failure Simmers flirts with.
key_cases.quote: the "existing Indian family exception" is no longer a viable doctrine applicable in Oklahoma insofar as Indian child custody proceedings are concerned

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody, that section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and that section 1915(a) does not bar an adoption when no preferred placement has come forward.
key_cases.relevance: It defines when the omission of active efforts is not an ICWA compliance failure at all, and it is the decision Simmers applies in Oklahoma.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.
